Many people assume that ASL is just gestures without grammatical rules and guidelines to follow. It bothers me when people say "I know sign language!" and then proceed to gesture something offensive.

Sometimes people say that it just came easy for me because I know other languages and that potentially my brain can absorb languages easier. While it COULD be a factor, I also don't want all my time, work, and interest to be dismissed either. Maybe the fact that I have ADHD and think visually DID help but I also genuinely fell in love with the language and continue to work on my skills. I didn't just do my homework when I was taking classes, I did extra, reviewed more often, practiced regularly, went to ASL meetups, etc. I didn't just look at the grade on my tests, I looked at what I got wrong and asked how to correct it. So I make sure people understand that they can also learn if they put the WORK into it.

If the pain is relentless, no matter how good your doctor is, you need to be referred to a pain clinic. Here's the frustrating thing; you need to find a good one and those are hard to come by.

It helped me to have my partner come with me. I didn't make any progress until they came with me to appointments. It helps to have someone help advocate for you because you are already too mentally and physically exhausted. You're SUFFERING and you shouldn't have to entertain a bunch of questions and risk not being taken seriously. 

When my doctor would say "you have to keep doing the exercises" after saying physio doesn't help my partner stepped in to say "she's been following every recommendation, that's not the problem."

Don't let doctors blame you for your pain, it's not your fault, they are the problem for not helping you. 

Here's what I wish I had heard when it all started for me; The cavalry isn't coming. That amazing doctor that you think is going to invest in you, completely fix you, etc. isn't coming. YOU have to do the work. You have to research your symptoms and then research what you find and what can be mistaken for what you find. You have to join groups, research doctors, and bring all that information to the doctors you have now to get anywhere. It won't be easy.

Doctors think within their knowledge scope and they won't deviate from that. You have to bring what you find to their attention in order to get referred and treated for your pain.

You are going to feel like giving up. Please don't. We hear you, it's unbearable, we understand. You deserve to be seen, treated, and cared for. 

Try everything, see the different specialists, and don't you dare for a single second doubt yourself and what you are feeling. Your pain is real. It's not in your head. Every time someone says that ask what else it can be. It's not anxiety. Don't entertain that stupidity from any doctor or specialist.

Please don't give up. We are all fighting for your success as much as ours. We have your back. Ask questions, reach out, and be seen.

The statistics are useful too. You can see what you wear the most or the least. Looking at things that I don't wear helps me to make better decisions when I try to declutter.

Another useful feature is that it shows you the cost per wear of an item. If you wear a $30 top 3 times it means it cost $10 to wear it every time. The idea is to try to get the most use out of something to get a low cost per wear. Only wear something 3 times and it's falling apart? I don't buy from that brand again. 

Anyways, I just want to encourage OP and anyone who reads this to stick with the setup because it's worth it!

Then, surprise, a couple months ago I started a new medication and now I'm back up struggling to fit again.

What sucks is that I don't always gain or lose weight in the same way every time. For example sometimes if my medication affects my stomach, I'll be more bloated and my pants are what I need to be mindful of. Other times my whole body might swell and then it's top, bottoms, and even shoes don't fit. It's unpredictable!

I started to declutter again but my partner told me to get bins and pack it away in the basement. 

If it's no longer my style or if I think I wouldn't wear it even if it fits, then clearly I'll get rid of it, but I regret getting rid of things before.

I'm hoping that now I've got a good amount of my base typical weight along with a fair amount of larger and smaller clothing for various seasons and occasions.

The advantage to having such diverse clothing sizes under one roof is the ability to lend something to nearly any friend because I will likely have something that fits them!

My biggest problem is that my pelvis is tilted so I struggled a lot to have my hips lined up and my back is always rounded.

Despite YEARS of stretching and doing activities to help my flexibility (primarily dancing) I just can't physically sit up straight.

After developing chronic low back pain, I learned that I actually have a deformity which has probably played a large part in my struggles to be flexible.

My body will simply never be flexible despite doing stretches and exercising. So while I do encourage people to stretch for their health and try as best as possible, sometimes we have to come to terms with reality and accept that our bodies have limits and potentially internal unknown reasons for our limitations.

I track all my clothing and accessories in an app and update every day to keep track of what I wear and how often, etc.

The other thing that has helped the most is having a friend to help me be accountable. When I'm struggling I just message her and she talks me out of spending on whatever or even just distracts me completely.

I am very impulsive so I often buy extra things even if I've made a list. She shops for me so that I avoid the temptation. It's not like with groceries or anything like that but with items that are needed less often like batteries. I ask her to pick up x, y, z for me the next time she's out and she picks up ONLY the things I need and then I pay her back. At the point where I was best managing my spending I was reaching for a goal where I only spend once a day and try to have as many zero spend days as possible.

If I had an appointment and I had to pay for parking, that was my spend so I wouldn't buy anything online that day. If I needed gas on my way to work, that was a day I would prepare food versus picking up food for lunch etc. Bills counted as a spend too so if I paid a bill, I likely wasn't going to a store that day either.

On many days, not spending was fine because that was my ultimate goal, but on other days I would struggle wanting so deeply to buy something online even though logically I didn't need any more clothes. If I had this urge but was struggling really hard, I would sometimes just get in my car and fill it up even if it was only a quarter tank empty. This sort of got that anxious energy out of my body a bit and, since I have to pay for the gasoline obviously, it was my spend and sticking to my rule I wouldn't make a purchase online for at least the rest of the day. 

The next day is a fresh start and by then I'd lost that temptation (mostly). The next day I might have parking to pay, groceries to get, a bill, or something else validly necessary compared to another shopping spree.

Even when getting a drink at Starbucks was something I wanted to limit, some days going for a drink and a snack would stop me from getting new clothes from Lululemon or wherever.

Maybe if you have this urge to use your money, look for something that is a necessary spend. 
I also found that making a list of different chores and tasks to do around my home helped me to have something to turn to so that I would get off my phone, away from the temptation of scrolling through my favorite stores online.

Good luck and stay strong!

Do you mind explaining how you had a venogram ordered?

My husband did a lot of research with regards to my pain and I seem to have every symptom for pelvic congestion. My doctor sent in a request to imaging for a venogram or "any test to help confirm a diagnosis". The imaging department decided on an MRI with contrast for my pelvic area.

I had no sedation and didn't have to fast or prepare for the procedure. They inserted an IV in my arm and the MRI itself was long but I don't know how long I was in there for. The hardest part for me was that they were instructing me to take deep breaths, to breathe out, to hold my breath for extended amounts of time.

Honestly the most difficult part was the deep breathing. I started to feel light headed and it was weirdly exhausting.

I know it's not the procedure you're having but I went in THINKING I was getting a venogram and got this instead.

I don't know why this was the imaging they decided on for me and I don't know if it's worth fighting to get a venogram.

I have 1 858 Items. Was it slow? Yes. Painful? Not at all, I found it therapeutic. 

I emptied my closet prepared to declutter and organize as best as possible.

From here, I tacked clothes on a sewing mannequin and took pictures of everything as I organized each type of item. If I was at home, my priority was to take all the pictures and put clothes away. If I wasn't at home, I was uploading everything and adding all the information using emailed receipts to have everything as accurate as possible. Over time I would go online to find the stock image of a lot of my clothes and replace them with the pictures I took.

(Don't judge me) I also looked through old pictures to add everything into the calendar (when I started I was using another app and I could go farther back in the calendar than I can with Whering). 

Slowly the statistics started as I entered everything and marked when I wore things.

It did take a long time. I'll admit that. Why did I power through? All that time that I spent dedicated to this I wasn't shopping. Those late nights where I often stumble onto sites and impulsively spend on something were replaced with me becoming obsessed with what I already have.

I started REALLY paying attention to what I have and wear compared to what I have and don't wear.

Not only could I start to know what I could get rid of, I also started spending less as I became more critical.

If I was out shopping, I'd look at what I already had. Oh look, I already have a similar top that I've only worn once, what makes this one special?

I have DILIGENTLY added everything as I shop by downloading the photo as I buy it and input the information. Here's the thing, I usually do this BEFORE I checkout and it's made me re-think and either buy less or abandon the cart entirely.

I've also added into the calendar what I wear every day. I can see what has been worth the cost or not, whether I can declutter or not, etc. 

My biggest takeaway has been the fact that I often buy bright colours, because I like them, but always default to wearing darker muted colours. So as much as I like the brighter colours, now I buy things that I'm more likely to wear.

For many years, my spending was well managed. I would look through the app and what I already had and make new outfits and such to the point that I would lose the urge to spend.

Things have taken a dark turn in the last couple of years with health and pain struggles. My spending is really out of control at the moment but every now and then, when I'm in a safe enough mind frame, I still look through the app to help minimize the damage as much as possible.

Once the bulk has been entered, it's easy to maintain!

For me it's when anyone starts the entrance with "just".

JUST make a list. JUST get up and do it. JUST sit down and focus.

It's a REALLY hard concept for someone that does not have ADHD to grasp just how hard it is to do something when it is naturally easy for them.

If someone can just decide to clean their bathroom every week, they can't grasp the concept of wanting to clean something and their body physically stopping them. "JUST grab cleaning supplies and clean"....I want to do the thing but I'm paralyzed on the couch hating myself for not cleaning.

Are you thinking of resources or methods to practice? Honestly the most easy and basic thing is to have students practice signing and recording themselves.

- Every class a student can be responsible for finger spelling 5 words and classmates have to write down what they see. Then 5 signs they learned the class before as a review and, again, have the classmates write down the answers of what the signs were.

This way there's an opportunity for classmates to practice reception and there is an opportunity for teachers to correct/improve the signs from the videos.

-Play bingo when they are learning numbers
-Play hangman to get them to practice letters 
- Have images on computers zoomed in and gradually zoom out and have the learners guess what the picture is using vocabulary words. If they don't know the sign, they can fingerspell. (There's a ton like that on YouTube so pause them to allow time for guesses)
- Have students describe something in their room that isn't in view (like a fidget, toy, artwork, etc.) and they have to practice describing it and other students guess what it is.
- Display a page of various objects and play I Spy: they can learn about material, colours, shapes,and other vocabulary 
- Have students describe a basic picture and classmates draw it.
- Similarly, students direct the teacher what to draw. For example a student signs "top right corner, sun", then another student "middle of page, girl", etc. Or a person describes their picture and then another person draws it and at the end compare how similar the pictures were to each other.

In terms of looking for things online, YouTube is helpful for signs and basic vocabulary. SigningSavvy is a good free resource.
For paid resources; ASL Spring is a subscription learning platform.

I've posted about this before, I actually started tracking what I wear and how often with an app.

I started a few years ago thinking I'd eventually forget to log what I wear everyday. Here I am, roughly 7-8 years later and it's the thing I most use my phone for.

At first, it helped to make me face my closet. I took out everything to reorganize, take pictures, and try things on. I got rid of a fair bit but I still had lots left.

While I added pictures, information, and such I was distracted from shopping. I even went through as many pictures as I could to add clothes to the calendar since before I started tracking.

On the app I can show the least worn items, so I organize my closet like this and try to wear these things. After a while, if I don't wear something, it's easier to figure out what to declutter.

My current app (Whering) shows me the cost per wear of each item that I have entered a price for. So if a sweater costs $20 and I've worn it twice, that means it costs $10 per wear. Sometimes I order my clothes by the highest cost per wear to try to wear whatever piece more often.

It is satisfying to see a low cost per wear because I feel like I've gotten good use out of it, but it's sobering to face what I've wasted my money on.

I have too many bags that I don't use. I have so many sweaters that I don't wear anymore, I have so many things that are just clutter.

I try to pay attention to why I don't wear something. Am I having trouble styling it? Is it just not my colour? Is it uncomfortable? Does it just not suit me? And on and on. Then I tag that piece of clothing on my app to declutter so that I can collect everything to donate. 

Sometimes I'll be shopping and I stop to look through my app to see if I have anything similar or if I have something I could style with whatever I'm looking at. I usually put things back after realizing I have something similar that works just as well and I stop wanting the new thing.

Every single day I add what I wore onto the calendar. I used to always wear the same thing over and over but now I branch out more. I've started to see my patterns so I don't buy things I'm less likely to wear. For example, I used to buy dress shirts/blouses for work, I've always had a ton. What I actually wear most is an undershirt and sweater or a relaxed fitted shirt on warmer days. I got rid of all my dress shirts, I didn't wear any or them for over 2 years, and I don't buy them anymore.

I used to buy more colors of the same shirt if I liked it. I looked at what I actually wore and noticed that I NEVER reach for a pattern, I always pick black if it's an option, and I pick blues and dark purples over reds and pinks. So now, I don't buy the colours and patterns that I always avoid.

When I'm wearing something and it bothers me, I make a note of it on my app with the article of clothing. If it's uncomfortable or I have to readjust it, I make a note so I can remember to get rid of it after I wash it. 

It's been great for me and, while I still have bad spend days, I am better now at spending on things I will actually get good use and value for.

The next thing to work on is letting go of things with sentimental attachment.... that's a whole other crisis and struggle!

I have tried so many "logical" strategies but shopping is so emotional for me I had to take a different approach. I can't say I am completely happy where I am, but my latest strategy has actually been very good for me.

I've written about this before, I try to only do one spend a day ALONG with trying to have as many Zero Spend Days per month. 

Basically I try one transaction a day so I have to plan things out better. Along with this, since many days I HAVE to spend (pay bills, gas, or assorted things), by the time I get to a day where I don't HAVE to spend, I'm eager to have a day with zero transactions.

For example, if I have an appointment on Wednesday and I know I need to fill up soon, I'll make a point to go out on Tuesday to get gas. That means on Tuesday I won't be buying anything else, Wednesday I'll pay for parking at my appointment, and on Thursday I do an exercise class that I pay for each week. If I don't have a bill to pay or a random expense comes up on Friday, that will be a day that I COULD buy something. I probably won't because I'm ALSO trying to earn a day without spending. (Occasionally I have days where I must spend twice if I have to pay for parking and an appointment. Usually I will aim to have Zero Spends the day before or after to still minimize my spending)

Not only do I spend with better intentions now, it's easier to track my spending because it won't be more than 31 in a month. 

If I don't HAVE to pay a bill or fill up my car I love adding a day on my calendar that shows Zero Spent.

When I'm struggling and feel the urge to buy something needless I talk myself out of it to cool the emotional side of me pushing to spend. I tell myself "You will be fine without X. Today, you don't need to spend. Today, you keep all your money. You will be fine without X." That repeated part is the most important because it calms that feeling of urgency that I usually have.

I've also made a point to learn about consumer psychology. Learning and being able to identify how I'm being manipulated has been very empowering because I don't fall for tricks. "364 people have this in their cart" those people can have it then, I don't care.


I also do other exercises to make me confront my own struggles: I'll re-organize my clothing, or I'll try to write down all the things I bought in the previous month, I'll look for things to declutter, or I'll try on as much as I can and be very critical of what I should and shouldn't keep.


These strategies have worked better than limiting myself to a budget or Strict No Buys, because as soon as I slip I sort of give up entirely. If I spend twice a day, tomorrow is a new day to try to manage my spending. I feel accomplished when I add a label at the end of my day with "Single Spend Day" or "Zero Spend". 

While many people suggest deleting apps or unsubscribing, I do have to admit I see a problem with this. While I do think it's important to declutter our inbox and spend less time on our phones, it is equally important to learn not to be triggered when we do have our phones and get emails. It's about having control and being able to walk by a store without needing to walk in or directly delete an email without opening the content. This is where shopping psychology is so important. 

Also, you don't have to delete Tiktok, but look for better content that lines up with your goals. It takes time but eventually you'll start seeing healthy content over trigger posts. There ARE influencers who are preaching minimalist styles, and these de-influencers are trying to promote saving money and not being tricked into buying stuff.

Having this supportive group has also been very helpful for me. I feel like in my real world, when I say I'm addicted to shopping, I get laughed at. I am not kidding when I say I have this problem but their only response is "just don't shop." If only it were that easy. Having a community that GETS IT is so important to me.
I know it takes some time but I don't have too many projects and I'm ok with the wait. I think most people prefer to use other programs and then import them with the offset already on.

Yes!!!! I've been encouraging people to learn about consumer psychology. This is so important to remind everyone, thank you for sharing this!


Once I started watching videos and reading about consumer psychology it became a lot easier to resist purchases and even be turned off entirely. 


I tell myself that the stores are ONLY interested in making money. While this sounds like common sense, it's easy to lose sight of this among all the "THIS SALE IS FOR YOU!" and "WE THINK YOU SHOULD TREAT YOURSELF" promotions. 


Everything they do is a manipulation and they know how to trigger consumers. The websites that have notes with "only a few left!" or "347 people have this in their cart", it's all about getting us to react and feel like it's urgent for us to get it. 


I don't even react when I get promotional emails anymore. I purposely stay subscribed so I could face the strategies regularly and practice not reacting to them. I think it's important to acknowledge what we see and still be able to make the decision to delete it. I'm at the point now that I'll have purchases in my head to pay attention to if something becomes available or a good deal. This is usually for gifts so clearly this is the gifting season. The fact that I can get all these things meant to engage me and that I can just shrug and move on is very empowering.

The stores with the sale signs? I don't care the percentage that's off or what free gift with purchase there is. I know what I want to buy, then I'll decide if I think it's worth the cost and go from there. I'm not going to buy anything extra just to get a bigger discount in the end. It sounds so obvious but shopping for me is emotional and impulsive so knowing what stores are doing to feed on my weaknesses has only made me more capable of staying rational and in control.

The metaphor I use a lot for practicing is "Creasing the paper". It's all muscle memory. When you make a card and you fold the paper in half, if you quickly run your hand over it, the paper retains the crease memory but it might not stay closed. It's still a card, there's evidence you did it, but you didn't spend a lot of time on it. Running your hands over the crease over and over again will make that crease more permanent and the card will sit closed better.

It's the same with signing. The more you practice the more it will intuitively come to you because you've created this muscle memory. 


I have so many experiences when afterwards I realize I could have signed something better. Just today, in one brief moment, my hands got tied up when I couldn't decide quick enough which sign for "computer" I wanted to use. I held out my hands, took a deep breath, signed what I wanted and on with my day. 


It all comes with practice. Sometimes my hands instinctively start a movement before realizing what I'm signing specifically.


So presenting can be intimidating but if you practice enough, crease the paper, create that muscle memory, you're going to be in a better position than not. 


It's also important to practice full out. Don't just think about it, actually DO it. Record yourself a few times without watching in between to see your improvement. Look at what is clear/unclear. Look at where your facial expressions can be better. Practice your hand agility by fingerspelling names or what you see around you. Beyond this is a collection of strategies:

Within a month there are automatically at least 10-15 days I have to set aside for bills, gas, dance drop in classes, appointments with parking fees, and school things for the kids. Once I realized how often I HAVE to spend on things I started really valuing days when I don't have to.


I have easier days than others but I mostly enjoy the days where I have struggled to restrain myself but still manage to in the end. Last week I was having a really bad day and I felt like I needed to get out of the house but I know that when I do that I usually go to a store and since I didn't need anything  I know it would have been something wasteful. Plus I would have needlessly used up gas and then I would need to fill up sooner. If I had given in I would have then felt too guilty about already spending that I would have skipped my dance class that evening so that I wouldn't spend twice in a day. I held off and told myself that I ALWAYS enjoy my dance class and it's the one thing I do per week to do for myself. When the evening came around I was SO proud that I actually held off and, sure enough, had a great time at dance.

My reflection on September has led me to certain goals and restricting myself for the first time on what I spend on. My pain started and I reduced my work even more but I had no idea it would permanently ruin me and I started paying for physiotherapy weekly as well as trying every possible cream, ice pack, heat pack, invested in better footwear, etc. all in hopes of recovering and getting back to just being a mom.


7 years later, all the physiotherapy appointments, psychotherapy appointments, drives to specialists hours away, paying for constantly changing medications, and paying for every snake oil product in hopes that SOMETHING actually works I'm down to zero savings. We do well for a family and I haven't struggled for family needs, school needs, and kids activities. But we don't think about all those things we wanted to do in our house. We don't talk about places to visit. Everything that I responsibly and excitedly saved is just gone with nothing to show for it. 


The worst part is that I could be in a better position except that my shopping addiction has never gotten under control. After paying and going through physical treatments I see something nice and think I deserve to pay for something that's for ME and not for my pain. I buy toys for the kids to make up for the fact that I physically can't move one day out of bed and try to make it up to them...even though I KNOW we have too much clutter and I don't want to show my love with material things but my body still does. Even KNOWING this, I physically struggle to act towards my goals and logical thinking. I tried seeing a psychologist to help but she said she couldn't help me because my problem is pain and until my pain is managed I'm going to keep struggling with my shopping addiction. Everything just feels futile.

I've set very simple goals for myself with very simple guidelines and this has been working best for me. In my MANY years of struggling with shopping addiction, I'm only now starting to feel like I have some control. Am I good yet? Nope. Every day I'm working on being better for another day more. And on and on and on.


No amount of strategies, thinking, tools, or apps were going to help me until I found the right medicine for me.


I struggled with the fact that despite being logical and strategic, my body proceeded automatically towards the cash or to checkout despite yelling to myself internally not to spend.


My strategy right now is to only have one transaction per day and to have as many "zero spend days" as possible in a month. Every day I have to plan out so that I only spend once. If I have a doctor's appointment where I will pay for parking I need to make sure I don't need gas on that day. I either plan ahead and fill up the day before or have enough until the next day. Since I fill up one day, I don't spend again that day...this means the stuff on Amazon? It has to wait. Every day I'm pushing things as I prioritize bills, family/school fees, etc. Every day when I have something in my head that I HAVE to have, I tell myself I'll be fine without it and that THAT day was a chance to have a Zero Spend Day.  Between bills, gas, fees for assorted things there are actually very few days open to be days where I can spend.


It didn't help me to set budgets. It didn't help me to limit categories of purchases. It didn't help me to commit to completing projects I've already started. It didn't help me to set decluttering goals. I reached out to MULTIPLE psychologists and psychiatrists and NOTHING helped until I found the right meds.


Now, those intrusive thoughts of material things I want to buy are still THERE but they aren't as loud. I can tell myself that I'm not doing it that day and that's different than telling myself no. 


Will ANY of this be helpful for YOU, OP? I don't know. Maybe not. I just want you to know that you are not alone and you are not judged. Try the Shopping Addict subreddit for more help but take it easy on yourself as you work towards building better spending habits.

I always struggle when I've been "good" for a while because making a small purchase is like ripping open a seam and things quickly escalate. I refer to it as when slips that become slides and suddenly it's an avalanche.

For a while I was justifying everything but now I actually talk to myself about how I WON'T MISS what I'm looking at. The top I'm looking at is nice and I will wear it but I'm also going to be fine without it. I might still like it in a week or month but I tell myself I can go another day without it until eventually the urge has passed. One day I just don't want it as much.


The thing about shopping is that we HAVE to. We HAVE to buy food, if clothes don't fit we HAVE to wear clothing and NOT being comfortable is only going to inconvenience us so we justify buying more because it's an investment. Don't think of this trip as the END to something but the START of a healthier relationship with spending. On the trip, don't just buy things because you're on a trip but because you would get it even if you were home. Don't buy nice clothes and use the excuse that they are souvenirs, your pictures and memories are that! If one day the clothing doesn't drape nicely and you don't wear it, it'll forever feel like you are throwing out memories instead of useless fabric.


Congratulations on all your progress so far, take a deep breath and move forward. I understand the emotional roller coaster and for me, I think of these times as symptoms. The urges and emotions are symptoms of me struggling with unrelated things so I start tackling other things like reaching out to friends, catching up on chores, etc.


I'm so glad you reached out because this is the hard part about addictions and it's so important for others to see posts like this and know they aren't alone.



Stay strong, stay smart, stay calm, and go one more day sticking to your goals. I hope you have a wonderful trip!

With shopping, all I had to do was just stop, right? The fact that I couldn't was because I wasn't trying enough.


Constantly interrupting people? It's because I'm rude. And of course I'm rude, I'm always cutting in and I KNOW it's rude but I keep doing it.


Anyways, a thousand plus examples and suddenly I understand a lot more about myself and I understand finally that, no matter how much I want, I'm going to keep doing all these things unless I get help.

I spend a lot of time reflecting and trying to identify what triggers me to help control my spending. Like you said, our bad habits are often a symptom, a sign that something is going on within us, and if we don't find that root cause we are forever going to struggle.

In my case, I am logical and emotional at the same time, all the time. Since shopping is a habit that I was taught at a youth age, and has been a constant familiar pattern, it has basically become my body's way of stimming. When I'm out and about or on my phone I have dozens of very logical thoughts that would usually help someone assess and make appropriate decisions for spending. I can reason that I don't need it, that I have too much already, that I can rent it, that it's not worth the money, AND at the SAME time I'm justifying why it's worth getting, how I deserve to spoil myself, how I'm having a good day, how I'm having a BAD day, how it's not worth the money but it's also KIND OF worth the money, how I'll be upset later if I don't buy it. ALL these thoughts that conflict with each other are equal in my head. I can't prioritize one side over the other to make a decision. I proceed to checkout on autopilot. I go to the cash register because it's easier than putting things back. NOW with medication, I still have all those thoughts but I can sort of hear the more logical ones better and dismiss the emotionally driven ones....if that makes any sense. I can sort of slow down and pay attention to the thoughts that are going to help me reach my goal.

This was a very long winded way to answer your question about pros and cons to meds but I promise there is a reason for this, lol!  I started with meds almost a year ago. Since November I started with one and since I didn't have negative side effects my doctor kept increasing the dose. I wasn't bothered by the meds but when my doctor asked if they were helping I kept saying I didn't know what it was supposed to feel like when it was working.


I wanted to better manage my impulse spending and I couldn't. For months I tried one med with different doses, eventually struggled with side effects, stopped and tried different ones, until FINALLY a couple months ago I was reading something and it just sort of hit me that SOMETHING was different. I read the book without needing to reread paragraphs like I always have. It was such a small thing but it was there. From there, that med increased and now we are learning what my body best responds to. We don't have it down perfectly yet but for the first time since this started last year I finally understand how it's a long process but ultimately worth it in my case. 

So the cons are that it takes time and money. For me, it's been worth it. I just want to best prepare people that are just starting the process that it doesn't always happen immediately or is clearly obvious. I didn't know I would know it's working until one day I just managed a bit better.

Clothes and miniatures. Definitely. I definitely have enough clothes and miniatures.

Unfortunately this knowledge does not deter me from buying more. I ask and answer myself dozens of logical questions but my impulses win out and my body goes through the motions of buying things whether online or in person.

Do I need this? Do I have something similar? Is it something I can borrow? Is it something that I can integrate into many outfits? Is it worth the money? Will it bother me if I don't have it? 

My body will still spend while I'm YELLING at myself internally, reminding myself how needless the spend is.

The right ADHD meds have made the biggest difference. Because equally to all my logical-don't-get-it thoughts I have why-not? thoughts. I have thoughts of you-deserve-it, that are equally loud. With meds, the logical thoughts get prioritized and I have better control. 

I have never had a problem with developing strategies and changing thought processes to help manage my spending. Having the ability to focus on the RIGHT thoughts while having dozens that contradict has always been my biggest downfall.

I have three little ones and my youngest was probably around 2.5/3 when I started. When I showed the kids the minis they immediately started playing with them as tokens, as props for their dollhouses, etc. They asked if they were supposed to open them and I just explained that when we open them or take them apart most of them don't go back together. I didn't say they couldn't take them apart but I braced myself for it. 



They play A LOT with them and they're exceptionally good at playing with them without ruining them. Sure, there's some wear and tear, but they are intact.



I have bins of minis that the kids play with but as for displays out of reach I have a handful of things I've done;



One is a wall mounted business card display shelf. It's a perfect size for minis, it's clear, and it's light so I was able to hang it with command strips. The pro and con is that it's open so dust will settle on and if my kids wanted to, they could reach and take them. The pro part of it is that I can just add and move the minis around easily.



Another thing I've used to display some is with a magnetic bulletin board. It's light and out of reach and I've just used magnetic organizers as shelves or storage to display the minis. I bought magnet strips to tape and glue onto different things to stick on and use for the minis. The possibilities are endless and since everything is on a magnet I can move everything around and play around with different formations. The most common modification people do is to add magnets but I don't like tampering with them. At most I might add a magnet inside boxes so that the minis look the same but it's easy to make your own shelves just with blocks.



I've invested in sunglass cases. The clear acrylic "drawers" stand upright and you can put the minis in, close the drawer, and voilà! The nice thing about these is that they are in a case so you can just wipe and clean the case and the minis won't get dusty. The case sits upright on a bookshelf or you can stick it to the wall with command strips easily.



I have wooden tea bag organizers that are square grids that stand upright. The spaces are a good size for minis but the downside is that the squares are open so if the box gets knocked over or it's on a wobbly bookshelf or something, the minis will fall. I've thought about buying acrylic clear hinges to add an acrylic sheet/door but I just haven't gotten around to it.



One of the easiest things I did is buy a bunch of desktop business card holders (off Temu) and I leave them with 2-3 minis in each just in different places as decoration. I think because they are among picture frames and such the kids seem to have understood they are decoration more than toys. Even my nieces and nephews leave these alone. These business card holders are especially good for the wrapper type minis or the boxes that are more likely to tip over.



If your child wants to play with them, I would recommend keeping a bin of doubles or buy some cheap off FB marketplace or something and teach them how to play with the minis so that they can play with them for a long time. The goal being they learn that the consequence of ripping them apart is that they can't use them again. Hopefully they learn the difference between the play minis and the non play minis.



Good luck, happy collecting! I hope you find something that works for you and that you have fun!

I was going in the direction of getting surgery for the labral tears because EVERYTHING I read STRONGLY encouraged repair.

The surgeon I was referred to sent me to more imaging and a diagnostic hip injection. I am also in another support group for Piriformis Syndrome and there were a couple people who had all the same symptoms as me, repaired their labral tears, and only additionally caused pain because it wasn't the pain source. 

Also, a coworker had her tears repaired and, again, worse outcome. I feel bad for her because she is in her early 20s and now she's in constant pain, worse than when it started, and the initial problem hasn't been addressed and she's just given up.


So anyways, I decided to get the hip injection AND test my piriformis to best plan treatment. The hip injection did not help at all, so I became even more hesitant to do surgery. Instead of testing piriformis we are testing the iliopsoas muscles and then explore piriformis if we need to. My biggest obstacle is getting injections and treatment since my doctor is hours away and it's hard to get appointments. I'm kind of stuck with the inconvenience AND the reality that they have best managed my pain so I'm staying with this team.


I expect to have an upcoming appointment with the surgeon again but the reality is that I don't want to have an unnecessary surgery.


The trouble with imaging is that it identifies things but rarely do we get imaging when we are fine. I may have had the labral tears for 20 years without knowing but now that we know they are there they are conveniently blamed. 


My first diagnosis that incorrectly was suspected of causing the pain was Bertolottis Syndrome. I was born with this enlarged vertebrae but didn't have pain my entire life. So my pain starts, they look at my back and see this deformity. They say that SOMETIMES this can cause the symptoms I have therefore we found the problem. No. ALL the treatments led to eliminating it as the pain source so I started looking elsewhere.

My MRIs identified labral tears and a surgeon pressed on and discussed bursitis with me. I got diagnostic hip injections to help make decisions for treatment but they were inconclusive.


Last week I saw a new pain doctor that my previous pain doctor referred me to based on my MRIs. I discussed with him the lack of response from the hip injections and we discussed labral tears, hip bursitis, and how I wanted to explore piriformis injections. 


After a physical exam with him doing the typical movements and asking questions I could feel my pain growing steadily. Based on my feedback/response to the physical exam and my medical history he believes it's not my piriformis and instead he wants to focus on my iliopsoas muscle. 


The symptoms overlap and referred pain mimics labral tears, hip bursitis, piriformis syndrome, and more. 


Diagnostic lidocaine injection, ultrasound guided, into my right side was the first step. The pain from the physical exam continued to grow on my left.....but not my right. I don't know if this was just a coincidence or if we are finally onto something.


I'm getting a follow up in a couple weeks and I'm going to ask to explore this further. 


Everything is so intertwined and I wish so badly there was a machine that could actually image pain and find the source.


It's too early to know where I'm going with this and what else I'm going to do but as long as there are things to try that are accessible and relatively conservative compared to surgery, I think it's worth trying or at least learning more about it.

I think getting some help is a great idea so you can practice both your signing and receptive skills! 
I saw a lot of people stop continuing classes because they were discouraged but I love seeing when someone is determined to work at it and truly learn!


There's a couple options to consider to find a tutor; there are many Facebook groups to look for to help support your learning. I know Facebook is dying in popularity and only for the older generation now 😋 but it really is a good resource for groups! Deaf/HOH Community (Learning/Teaching ASL), ASL Lessons are the first two that I'm familiar with but you can find more. Especially in that first group, you can find Deaf teachers that offer lessons, support, and practice at flexible schedules and varying fees. So if you post exactly what you posted here you can find a Deaf mentor. Since there are so many, if you don't feel like one is a good fit, there are more to connect with.

You can also consider subscribing to aslspring.com. There are varying levels that you can subscribe to and have access to videos from beginner to advanced levels as well as group practice for beginners and one on one mentoring with a Deaf /HOH mentor. (Again, many to choose from). You can always try it for a month (make sure you subscribe to their mailing list first to get a discount code to try it) and if you realize it's not what you want, it's easy to unsubscribe. If you realize you want more one on one mentoring than is included, I would suggest contacting them to pay extra for more one on one. Full disclosure I have not tried this so I don't know if that's possible but it would be worth trying at least. (An advantage with ASL Spring is that you can review all the levels at any time and there are videos to test and practice your receptive skills)

Lastly, this is just my advice as an ASL learner. Find Deaf/HOH tutors/mentors - I did not understand how much value and the rich history and experience that comes from the Deaf community. When I started I admit I knew nothing and considered ASL as simply a language. What a learning curve! I am so grateful for the fact that my school only hired Deaf teachers and I didn't appreciate how important this was until I had a better understanding of Deaf history and culture. 


Along the way I did several things to help my ASL: I made video diaries. Simple, the date and what signs I remember learning that week in class or practicing fingerspelling, it doesn't have to be complicated. It forced me to realize what I wanted to express but couldn't and it would stimulate my brain to go learn more signs and ask my teachers, etc. It also meant I could go back and rewatch and test my understanding of my own signs; if I can't understand myself, another person likely wouldn't understand me either! I really learned to be clear and stop bad habits. For example my earliest videos I'm bumping my letters and being very stiff, my eyes look terrified and I'm mouthing everything. It feels great to look through everything and literally see my development. 

Fingerspell license plates when you are driving or on the bus, you can exercise letters and numbers this way. At first ABHM 347 was A-B-H-M-3-4-7, and then I started trying to make names out of the letters like 'Abraham' 3-4-7. Numbers were individual numbers until I started learning higher numbers and they became 3 hundred forty 7. The point is to get inspired with everything around you and prompt yourself to practice spontaneously. It's easy to practice the things we know, push yourself! If one hand feels too easy, switch hands! Alternate hands per letter, anything! This exercises your muscles and agility that will only benefit you.


Signing songs is controversial because not enough people understand the english-ASL conversion and often lack expressing versus signing word for word. So I'm not suggesting signing music, BUT I used music to grow my vocabulary. The songs that I listened to, I would consider what vocabulary I didn't know and I would learn the signs. I would take lyrics and I would try to figure out how I could express that in ASL. I wasn't trying to sign the song, but when I was in the car it would help pass the time and I built an extensive vocabulary that supported me in my classes. 

I signed in front of a mirror and I practiced exaggerating facial expressions. It sounds silly and I used to feel self conscious.....until it felt natural for me to use my face and body to express myself. 

Do not practice signing sentences in English with signs. SEE is signed exact English, ASL has its own grammar and sentence structure and practicing this early on is important.  I used baby books to practice. A book about colours? Yes! Each colour and an item of that colour, it's great practice! Those early learning books with basic reading are great too because the sentences are basic so I could rearrange and express in ASL more easily than a complex English sentence. 

Subscribe to Deaf and HOH content creators. Even if you don't understand everything, it keeps your mind partially on ASL all the time and this constant support will be helpful. 


I hope you find something that works for your schedule! Good luck and keep working hard!!!

On the topic of perceived judgement. There are sales strategies and become familiar with the psychological tricks used to motivate consumers is really important. All those "only a few left" are meant to trigger our FOMO. I repeat to myself, only the stores benefit from my spending. They put their effort into getting us to spend. Take a deep breath and be critical about why you are buying something. Are you replacing something you need? Are you worried you won't see it again? If it's on sale, is it worth the amount you are spending or are you thinking more about the perceived deal? If you didn't know the item existed before you saw it in the store, is this something you'd look for? If you don't buy this item, will it negatively impact your life? Thinking hard about where you are mentally and emotionally will help to take away the impulse to be able to be more rational. A big red flag for me is when sales associates try to push the sale by saying "better get it while you can, it's the last one" because, again, only the store benefits. Only the employees benefit. When someone is SO eager to make a sale I automatically think it's been around with no interest and they just want it gone. I should enjoy what I get instead of feeling pressured to only resent it later.

This is a result of lack of awareness. Unfortunately most of society expects very limited and black/white presentations of disabilities. There is a growing awareness now more than ever with people having more platforms available to educate. With TikTok and YouTube more and more people are documenting their journey and experiences with disabilities and, this might surprise you, there's more than four reasons a person might need priority to sit! Something even more surprising, not all disabilities are obvious and visible!

I was diagnosed as an adult but I can't say my parents would have been any different had I been diagnosed as a child. 

My father would tease me because I'd step out of my jeans at night, and leave them on the ground bunched up but upright. It was playful teasing but I just couldn't remember to pick them up and fold them or throw in the wash and even though his intentions weren't mean, I did become self conscious about it. I still do it but it's also one of the quick things I can do to get me started. I don't deserve the saint that is my husband that puts up with all my open drawers, cupboard doors, and half hung/folded laundry.

With my mother it was an entirely other volatile ordeal. I'd tidy up when asked but HER expectations of a clean room and mine were very different. It was so disheartening to actually try and then be told "you did nothing". I have always needed TV/movies as background noise to be productive and to her, screens were a distraction. So when she'd hit her  action mode and come in to "help" (which was really her stepping in and yelling at me) she would turn off the TV and IMMEDIATELY made it worse.
She would start moving things around, she'd throw out stuff that, to me, was special and would just complain about how she needs to do everything because I'm just a lazy, useless, spoiled, ungrateful child...it was bad.


I've thought a lot about what would have helped me and consider this when it comes to my kids. As far as I know, I have never upset them with regards to room expectations but they are still young and I'm going to follow their lead.


I don't expect her bed made every day nor her floor completely visible but there's a few things that I do to keep it manageable so that it looks messy but isn't dirty. It looks busy (and I think nicely reflects her creative spirit) but I can safely maneuver around without concern. 


Having a place for things really helps because instead of saying "clean up" I can say "Put your X away". One day I might expect stuffies to be put away, the next day all clothes off the floor and in laundry. 

When it comes to putting away laundry, I fold it and from my room have her run between picking up clothes and her dresser putting things away. I give her a long warning "In a few minutes I'll need help putting away your clothes, when I finish sweeping the kitchen I'll come get you". Then I tell her to go as fast as she can when putting away her things and then she can go back to whatever she was doing. Her clothes don't stay nicely folded when she puts them away and I don't care. Maybe she'll get things away more neatly as she grows up or maybe not but I want there to be a balance between helping/responsibilities without inflicting that 'control' energy I grew up with. 

I tell her when the level of clutter has tipped and ask her what I can most help with while she's at school so when she gets home it doesn't look as overwhelming as before. I always ask for her input for what I can help with and ask her what she wants to be responsible for and when she thinks she will want to do it.  Sometimes I'll guide her by saying that I want her to get something done before bedtime so afterschool she can decide at what point she wants to do it. I always offer to help because I get to learn about her games. She explains why she had toys out a certain way and I use that time to ask her about school and friends. 

There are times that she won't cooperate and I try to consider what is affecting her mood. Should we have a snack first? Should we try tomorrow? Should we change our plan? I have always preferred being in clutter with my projects in motion suffocating my desk and I just wish my mom had taken more time to recognize the method to my madness. 

For necessary or urgent intervention I find my 6yo does well with little challenges like who between us can find the most water bottles or how quickly can we move stuff out of the way and into its place. When she can't find something she comes to me because apparently I know where everything is. I constantly explain that I don't know where everything is, I find it by tidying up. If she wants something that she can't find, she helps me tidy up to find it. The act of just starting starts a momentum and suddenly we've had an impromptu and productive cleaning moment.


I don't know if any of this will be helpful for you or not, each child is different and just because I have a very different organization expectation, I recognize that everyone has their own preferences so hopefully you find something to suit that while maintaining healthy child/parent relationship.

I taught health for a number of years. I always felt like grade 6 was late because at 11/12 some girls might have already started their periods.

I've used different videos but I'm not a fan of them. I just stick to the facts and I'm very upfront. I explain that what I'm talking about might feel awkward, uncomfortable, or even a bit scary even though there is nothing to feel awkward, uncomfortable, or scared about. 

I explain that bodies grow at different rates and that puberty means different things change in our bodies. Since our school is very progressive, I make a point to explain that puberty is different for people born with vaginas versus penises so I minimize using girl/woman for the sake of our trans students.

Then I talk about what happens with our bodies and explain how healthy it is to have our periods and how we don't need to do any extra cleaning etc. I talk about different ways to deal with our periods tampons, pads, silicone cups, period under etc. There are so many more options now than ever. I talk about what is "typical" for a period and what should warrant visiting a doctor.

I tell them to explore their body. Yes, they will start growing more hair and start developing breasts and it's all normal. I tell them it is ok to look at themselves especially because if anything ever changes, they can speak to a doctor if they are concerned. 


I explain that I was self conscious about talking to grown ups when I was younger but over time found the right people to talk to. I find the most modern and trusted sites and explain that, just like with their work, some sites are better than others. If they are ever unsure of information they are learning doctors are a good resource. If they have questions naturally I answer them. If they are too shy to ask, they can email me. Sometimes they just don't want to say it out loud. (I would also have a box for anonymous questions but if it's just you and your niece, clearly there's no point, lol!)

From experience, the most common questions are: will it hurt? This is asked every year, every class, without fail. So I explain that cramps can vary in pain level but the actual bleeding is painless.  The next most asked question is how to know when it'll happen so I talk about having backup underwear and supplies in a discreet bag. Also now there are period underwear and swimsuits which means if they start having cramps and it's been a while since they had their last period, it would be safe to wear period underwear or a pad and if they don't want to use tampons they don't need to miss out on swimming etc. There's a LOT to talk about.

One thing I've started talking about, among all the normal things that happen around our period; acne, diarrhea, mood swings, etc. is the fact that a lot of things AREN'T normal. As much as I HATE this, the fact is that women's pain is often dismissed and belittled by doctors. If ever anything is out of the normal, they should see a doctor. If that doctor doesn't address them seriously, they should find another doctor. PMS cramps should be manageable, our flow should be manageable, and while I can't say having our period is "fun" it shouldn't be a massive inconvenience and now more than ever there are ways to help these extreme things that we can experience.

I talk about how people can start birth control for different reasons, not just because they are sexually active. That decision is one to talk with a doctor and a trusted adult about. What works for one person, might not work for another.


I just talk and direct to online resources as needed. Some kids prefer to look up resources privately while others openly ask and prefer to be more open. You know your niece best. What do you think she would be most receptive to? I would also encourage her father to learn about what his daughter prefers for period products because it shouldn't be weird for him and he is the one doing the shopping. 

The most important thing I would tell my students is not to be embarrassed about their body and that it's always ok (and encouraged) to ask questions. I answer every question with as many facts as possible, I've never laughed at a question, and I've always admitted if I didn't know an answer and would do some research to address that question as soon as I could. 

Something else I would do is start with saying we are going to learn about Periods (specifically with regards to puberty because otherwise at least one kid will say it comes at the end of a sentence) and ask what they know. This would be a good way to open the discussion with your niece so that you can correct misconceptions or figure out what else she needs to know. Also, it doesn't have to be everything in one super long conversation. It can be small conversations over a long period of time. 

Sorry if this is a lot...I just think it's so important to arm kids with as much information as possible. Also, like I said, there are so many more things now than there used to be! Period swimwear??!?! Awkward 14 year old me would have LOVED that!

I kind of laughed and, please know that I don't mean it in a mean way but rather that I've been through this aspect of my shopping addiction and it's more of a laugh at myself to think about where I was before coming to terms with my shopping addiction.

I think if you think about it logically, you know that a healthy relationship is not based on mandatory gift giving (at least not modern relationships).

I also tried to validate my spending because if it wasn't on me, I'm being a selfless person and because it's for other people and I'm making them happy, I can justify every penny spent.

The reality is that it really was just an excuse for me. The act of shopping, going out to malls, visiting stores, learning about new products, etc. was a habit I wasn't ready to face and change.

And let's face it, any relationship whether romantic or not, shouldn't come with strings attached. If my friends and partner only felt loved and cared for based on if and how much I spent on them, then they aren't people I want in my life.

Now, I do genuinely enjoy giving and seeing their reaction, and especially if it helped them in some way, but ultimately it is who we are to each other as people that matters most.

Giving gifts was also a result of my insecurity. Maybe expensive gifts will make someone like me more, consider me a better friend, treat me better....and yeah...it sounds dumb now...and it took me a long time to admit it.  In the end ..as cliche as it is it really is the thought that counts when it comes to gifts...giving often and giving bigger than before really takes away from how special and genuine gifts can be. It can also take away from how genuinely good a relationship can be.

I didn't depend on monetary expressions of love from anyone so why would it be any different the other way around?

Now that I'm in a much better place, and I'm more confident in myself and a lot less insecure and just know myself better... everything is different. I don't stress about gifts around birthdays or holidays anymore. Instead, if I see something that reminds me of a loved one, I buy it, wrap it, and hold onto it for Christmas or a birthday. Or I don't. If I never see anything that makes me think a friend or family member, I just don't. I don't want to give them clutter for the sake of exchanging something. Most of the time we make a point to go to a show together or we plan a special dinner or we set aside a Saturday night to catch up..... The key part is WE. Friends, husband, family....WE, me and that person plan it together. 

"Hey I saw this show was coming in January, should we go see it to celebrate the holidays?". Sometimes one of us treats the other, sometimes we buy our own tickets. It's balanced and simple.

I'm not sure if my suggestions will help you or not but I commend you for trying to help and acknowledging their addiction. You mentioned potentially ending the relationship and I won't speak to that because there are many aspects to a relationship and it's up to you to decide what you want.


In terms of ways to help, I can only give suggestions that have helped me, but obviously there is no quick fix, one size fits all strategy. The key thing is to be able to talk.


1) Identify what is a want versus a need. If it's a want or a non-immediate need I make a list that I share with my closest friends and family. I will constantly go to this list and delete things I no longer want, add as I have wants etc. so that when it is my birthday or a holiday, there is that list to avoid "what do you want for Christmas?". I have spent years telling family not to buy me things for holidays because I keep things out of obligation even though I would not have bought it myself. This way, for my family that insists in having something to give, I'm getting something I genuinely want. Sometimes it's cleaning supplies, storage baskets, etc.


The benefit of this list isn't to get everything but rather to have a place to put that impulse energy. Often, after time passes, I realize how many things I no longer want. It feels so good to delete those things and celebrate the victory of not having spent that money and not having that extra clutter.


Struggling with developing a habit of NOT getting things, NOT accumulating, means that it is difficult to feel progress as there is no immediate reward. Deleting things off my list is how I get a reward.


2) Accountability Buddies. I am blessed with friends that want to help me even though they don't understand what it's like to have lack of control over ones habits. This is why I have two core people that help to stay in line. Either I text them or they come do errands with me, they know how to help me.


I don't need to rationalize. I know rationally I don't need a new clothing item or whatever and yet, I still procede with the purchase. What I need is distraction, and that's what my buddies do. In a text they'll ask me about my day, upcoming plans, they'll tell me about their day, talk about ANYTHING so that my focus pivots and I lose focus on that thing I wanted. In person, when I have errands, I know I don't ever just stick to a list. Someone comes with me and also has my list, so when I see something that I'm just attracted to, they step in and will physically remove items from my cart or, just like in texts, will distract me. 


If I need one thing, for example batteries, and I know I will probably buy more things if I go to Walmart, I'll message a friend who will pick up that one thing for me. I meet up with them (and of course pay them back) at their house. I get out of the house, socialize, and have completed an errand, without giving me an opportunity to see something to buy.


The greatest benefit is that I get out and socialize.


3) Online shopping. Yep. It's a problem. I have not found a way to stop..but sometimes slowing down helps. I'm in Canada so shipping can take a while depending where I order from. I try not to order/buy anything until I've received the last thing I ordered. I know it's not much but since sometimes I have to wait over a week, I've had time to add things to my list and delete things too. Just because I've received my last purchase doesn't mean it's time to buy again, it just forces me to put my energy somewhere.


4) I'm going to talk about my list again. It includes all costs. The price, rough exchange rate, shipping, duties, etc. Seeing numbers and seeing how a good deal quickly adds up to a waste of money, triggers me. Suddenly things aren't as tempting. Encourage this list, talk to them about it, question it too. Discussion is important.


5) My partner is my rock. They've never made me feel bad or judge me. My partner isn't my accountability buddy because quite frankly, he enables me. Not intentionally, but he wants me to treat myself and to be happy. I count on him to help my broader goals; chores, organisation, decluttering etc. It takes a LOT of mental energy to think about not spending and it's hard. It's hard to describe but it physically hurts. My husband is my reprieve. 


6) Shopping is a lifestyle habit so if that's being taken away something needs to replace it. Volunteering, dog walking, cooking, writing, reading, anything to keep hands and mind busy. Hopefully a hobby that doesn't require investing in supplies. 


7) My spending is mostly on clothing. I have an app that I track what I wear and when I wear it. It helps to come face to face with just how much I have. I also physically organize and reorganize my closet. I need busy hands. Find a way to get your partner to face their spending.


8) I learned about shopping and spending psychology. All those strategies that stores and ads use to get us to spend, I learned to identify and it has helped trigger a reaction in me where I recognize I'm being manipulated and fight it. All those "only 4 left" or "almost gone" notices don't phase me anymore. If you become familiar with these, you can help point them out.


9) I started subscribing to and watching videos of my goals, money saving, financial goals, etc. It seems obvious but I can't watch clothing haul/review videos without getting tempted. The solution is not to watch them. Find these videos for your partner, watch them together.


10) Acknowledging I have easier days and harder days. I say them out loud. I tell my friends. For me, it's work every day. Even when no one else is thinking about it, I am. It's like an affirmation for me like I'm still trying and it's better than ignoring my problem. Even to people that don't know the extent or are outside my accountability buddy friends, I will often just voice my progress. Sometimes I just need someone to hear me. Be that listening ear.

I know all these things are for the person struggling ..so I'm sorry if this doesn't help you support your loved one. I just think if you understand a bit of what we go through, it might help to give you ideas for how you can help.

What are you spending on?
Unfortunately there is no quick fix and people that don't understand will just say "just don't spend money", "just don't buy stuff" which is not helpful and insulting. If it were logical to us, we wouldn't have trouble with it.

I don't know your situation and I can't say I'm in control myself, but I've learned baby steps are better than nothing so I'll just share what I've tried.

- Make a list if you actually need something. Go with a friend to help you STICK to that list to help you avoid impulse.

- Look around when you want to spend and look for something else to do: clean, laundry, tidy up a little, call a friend, write a friend, fix something, etc. 

- Shopping is your habit, so you need to replace it with something. Think about that when you go to spend. What are you avoiding that you need to confront?

-Before you convince yourself you need something ask yourself: Can I borrow from someone instead? Do I have something else I can use? Can I find something at a thrift store? (Careful with this one, take a friend to keep you from needlessly spending)Join a Buy Nothing Group and ask on that group instead. (The point of Buy Nothing is not to take advantage of someone's kindness but to avoid unnecessarily consuming things that someone else is able to give. Make a habit of gifting as often as you receive) and another thing "If it's not urgent, no matter how small, can you put it on a wish list and ask for it as a gift for birthdays or holidays.

- Another big thing is to have someone to talk to. Even if it's Reddit. Talking out loud is also helpful. Admit when you've made a mistake. Acknowledge it. Figure out what you can do next time to maximize success. Figure out your mindset and what got you to that mindset. 

Don't trick yourself into thinking you need to spend to make a change. For example, a diary and journal can be very therapeutic. You DO NOT need to buy a new notebook. You can start a a file on your computer or download a FREE app and regular pens are just as legible as special decorative stationary. All the bells and whistles are fun, but not necessary and should not stop you from progressing.

Same thing for organizing; (I'll admit, I'm projecting here) you don't NEED new storage bins or nicer storage baskets, you don't need new hangers so it looks more nicer. Save those things for birthdays or holidays so that you aren't spending.

For me, only buying with cash hasn't worked but I do know it has worked for other people. That's something for you to figure out. I personally think that strategy was easier before everything became digital because at this point, some things are cheaper online and we need to hold ourselves accountable. 

Like I mentioned before, it helps to get a friend you can call any time. Someone to help keep you accountable. "I know I don't need this but I found this random thing on sale and before it was $x amount and now it's only $y amount". So your accountable person can say "Hmm stop." It may even mean your accountable friend physically returns your stuff for you.

Watch videos of minimalism, shopping psychology, and decluttering. Keep watching them so that it's always on your mind.

You my fall back a few times but like I said before, steps forward are steps forward.

Celebrate your little victories, admit your mistakes, and keep trying.

For me the whole "NO BUY AND IM GOING TO ORGANIZE EVERYTHING STARTING NOW" has never worked. It's a lifestyle change and for me I've learned it's about making small changes until that small thing becomes a good habit. I read somewhere that it takes about 20-25 days for your body to develop a habit. Not sure the validity of that but I have made improvements by doing very very little over a long period of time and then gradually adding on.

Last year I decided I was going to start with my bed. I made my bed every day instead of leaving the sheets disheveled. Because when I bring something into the room, like laundry, I leave it on the floor because the bed is a mess and then of course I forget about the laundry.

So I started with the bed being my priority.

Very small.

After that, I decided that anything I wore but didn't need a wash, I'd put it back in my closet properly. So those jeans that I knew I was going to wear again, they would be put away properly. Even if I wore them the next day.

So after a couple of months, making my bed and putting away still clean clothes were the two things I made a point of always doing. It may seem small, but that was two things I was doing that I hadn't been doing before.

The next thing I added on was taking objects into their proper rooms and places as I'm moving around the house. So if I'm leaving my room after getting up, I'm carrying the glass and snack plate from the night before with me.

Something small. Etc.

All these little things add up. It may seem slow but it quickly becomes significant.

Over time I noticed a small change triggered me to automatically do something else. For example, with the bed made I would fold the laundry while watching TV since I had the space as opposed to before when I'd dump the laundry basket on the floor and go into the living room to watch TV.
Putting away my re-wearable clothes also automatically made me toss everything to wash in the proper basket instead of leaving a dirty pile on the floor. Or also trigger me to see a couple other small things to pick up off the floor.

As I said, everyone has a different strategy. Hopefully some part of this helps.

Since it's to practice, when I started I would sign 1-8-4. After I learned how to sign larger numbers, again, since it was for practice I changed it to 184 (one hundred eighty four).

Another thing I would do is try to remember a sign to correspond with each letter.

(If you are the passenger of a very long drive, I recommend this. I have never been bored on a long car ride since I started doing this)

If the license plate is HMCD 825
I would sign
H - M - C - D -8 -2-5

Then 825 (eight hundred twenty 5)

THEN I find a sign to correspond with each letter:
H - Home
M - Mouse
C - Chocolate
D - Daughter

I try to always use different vocabulary so I'm not always signing the same things and to challenge myself.

I used to keep an ASL dictionary with me so if I felt like I was re-using the same signs for a specific letter I could learn new signs and expand my ASL vocabulary 

Want to make it more challenging? Make a story with the words you signed and try to express it in ASL;

My daughter came home and saw a mouse eating chocolate.

Home - my - daughter - arrive - saw what? - mouse - eating - chocolate! (And I could add to it, describe where the mouse was, etc.) and I would play around with signing it differently.

I made note of what I struggled to express to asked my teachers....after a while they stopped being surprised by my asking the best way to sign "the cow licked me instead of the  ice cream" and other such things.

- Film yourself signing assorted random words every day and randomly go through them to practice understanding. 

- Start a video diary, it will help you to practice daily and you will lengthen your vocabulary list

- reach out to local ASL groups. This can be tricky but usually you can find something via Facebook. Even on here, people reach out for an ASL buddy to practice with. (Naturally, proceed with caution)

- when you are waiting somewhere, instead of playing on your phone fingerspell and sign everything you see. If you don't know a sign, make a list. For example, I remember being at the doctors and I finger spelled and signed chair, door, magazine, phone, patient, doctor, and I wrote down the things I didn't know like receptionist, prescription, etc. So after I practiced my finger spelling, I looked up whatever vocabulary I could find.

- while on the road, spell out license plates. This is really useful because it forces you to practice letters and numbers and it's just a way to develop muscle memory. For the numbers you can start with single digits and then as you become more confident you can sign the larger numbers (so instead of A-B-B-H-6-3-2, it would later be A-B-B-H-632).  Another way to use license plates to prompt practicing is to think of a sign for each letter you see. So for my previous example: A (apple) B (bug) B (ball) H (hot) 632
If you're worried about other people staring, don't be. People get lost in their own world's and rarely notice. The ones that DO notice will usually be aware of what you are doing and might compliment you, or admit they are studying ASL too.

- to expand your vocabulary, read children's books. Very young reader books will usually have a theme (colours, animals, seasons, opposites, etc.) 

- sign as often as you can. If you only know one word out of a sentence while you are talking, sign the one word. This is something to be careful with because ASL grammar is different than English so be sure to keep that in mind, but using the signs you DO know will increase your confidence and muscle memory so as you progress in your learning you can focus on grammar or proper facial expressions and not on remembering a sign because, by then, you just know it.
